newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche Bank on course as Kopper bows out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche Bank on course as Kopper bows out.

text.p: Hilmar Kopper formally stepped down as Deutsche Bank AG chief executive on Tuesday presenting a 28 percent rise in first-quarter pretax earnings and declaring the bank well on the way to becoming a global player.

Kopper told shareholders at Deutsche's annual general meeting that pre-tax profit rose to 1.29 billion marks from 1.0 billion in the first three months and predicted earnings in the full year would also grow.

Kopper, 62, was due to move up to chair the bank's non-executive supervisory board after the meeting. He is being succeeded by Rolf Breuer, an eloquent investment banker who has been on Deutsche Bank's management board since 1985.

Praised by shareholders for steering the bank through seven difficult years, Kopper said the first quarter figures "...confirm our estimation that the current financial year is going well and that we will again be able to report an improved result for the year as a whole."

Profits in the first quarter were driven by bullish financial markets which led to a 43.6 percent jump in trading profit to 1.0 billion marks. Net commission income rose 18.1 percent to 1.98 billion marks.
Operating profit after provisions for bad debt rose 21 percent to 1.37 billion marks.
Administration costs rose 15.3 percent to 4.25 billion marks, reflecting the cost of the bank's continued expansion into investment banking.

Kopper, who took over as chief executive in 1989 after his predecessor Alfred Herrhausen was murdered by Red Army Faction guerillas, reiterated the bank's goal was to become "one of the world's leading modern universal banks" and said it was making rapid progress.
He also predicted Deutsche's return on equity would rise to 25 percent before tax by the end of the century from 17.1 percent in 1996.

"We would almost have reached that goal last year without our mishap in London," Kopper said, referring to irregularities at London-based fund arm Morgan Grenfell Asset Management which cost Deutsche 1.2 billion marks.

Kopper said that Deutsche's swift action to compensate investors for losses resulting from the mismanagement of three European unit trusts by fund manager Peter Young had enabled it to avoid losing customers.

"We no lost no customers. More attention was paid to our positive action than to the human failure." Young was dismissed and four senior Morgan Grenfell officials also quit after the affair which came to light in September last year.
Kopper said that after years of expansion, the bank may now cut back some of its activities that do not meet the required level of performance.
"Size and breadth of business are no longer a quality stamp, and they are certainly no guarantee of success. Today's competition demands that we are quick and agile."
Analysts said the first-quarter results were in line with expectations. Deutsche's shares closed down 1.62 marks to 97.08 marks.

"1997 is still a year of restructuring for the bank and the markets are benefiting Deutsche via strong growth in its trading and commission income," said Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank.
"The bank will earn the fruits of its expenditure on investment banking in the coming years."
Deutsche's shares closed floor trade down 1.5 percent at 97.18 marks, broadly in line with the overall market.
